author: @michaeli1440
comment: Having tested the Audi, BMW, Mercedes and Porsche - this is lazy journalism.  The Porsche is the best for build quality and handling (be it hybrid or sport / sport plus mode).  All three and the Mercedes are over priced regardless and therefore 'quality for money' is thrown out of the window as buyers would look elsewhere if that was the priority.  As for the weight and brakes - none of these cars as exactly sports cars.  All are SUVs and weigh accordingly.  The Mercedes is great if you are looking for a boat feel.  The BMW is probably the car closest to the Porsche.  Having owned both a BMW X5 and a Porsche Cayenne, I would say that the Porsche is simply in a class above the BMW and the others in this comparison - be it the hybrid model or any of the pure petrol engines.  In truth though, all these cars really make no sense so whichever someone chooses to buy is likely down to subjective rationale rather than common sense.

author: @wladimirb1506
comment:
Leased a 2026 Hyundai Tucson N-Line X 1.6 150 hp FWD petrol since 11/25, driven 3,000 km so far:

Pros: great design, excellent interior quality (N-Line), lots of space, good acceleration, top-notch infotainment, strong matrix headlights, very good Krell sound system, comfortable seats, and the panoramic roof is a nice touch. The suspension feels nicely agile without being floaty, yet still very composed on rough roads.

Cons: fuel consumption is higher than expected: around 9 l/100 km mixed, 6.0 l/100 km is possible at 100 km/h, but on longer motorway trips at 130 km/h it’s hardly ever below 8.5 l/100 km. The lane-keeping assist keeps the car too far to the left, which feels uncomfortable. The automatic transmission reacts slowly: shifting from D to R feels like it takes 1.5–2 seconds, and when pulling away there’s first a short delay, then a sudden, jerky surge of power. The throttle is also tuned very aggressively in the 0–20 km/h range. Maybe it will improve as the system adapts, but right now it still feels rather poor.

Conclusion: I would choose it again. For me, the overall balance works.

video_title: We Tested Ten SUVs, Which One's the Best?
author: @cd7856
comment:
Nicely produced, but the reviews seem overly focused on infotainment, not on price, quality, safety features or crash test ratings.

I like the Tuscon. I actually rented one for a week this year.  Fuel economy, price, performance, features, infotainment, yada-yada, all pretty good.  But, the  trim level I had didn't have some current safety features and the Tucson's IIHS crash test ratings are not quite as good as others.   So,  it is a no for us.

The Sorento isn't bad.  Nice, quiet, fuel efficient, good infotainment, nice design, fuel efficient, good ride...   I just cannot stand the climate control being merged with other stuff.  Very hard to use.  Kind of a deal breaker.   Also, the car also feels a bit small.  So, not buying it.     But,  safety features are great.  Haven't checked out the crash ratings.    

The Rav4...  Two major complaints 1) A car is for driving. The thing is so lethargic.  You guys are totally right -- It is like a bigger Prius!     How can you enjoy driving it?  I mean, I owned a Prius and it was great, but so unresponsive.    I would be afraid to have my wife pull onto a busy road driving this thing.  A definite no!      2) The inside is small.   The front feels more likea pod/cockpit than an open space and the rear seats are small.   If you're above 6ft, good luck....     I test drove a couple Rav4s.   The rest of what the guys say is true, but man,... 

The CR-V is pretty good unless you are into towing.    Main concern would be the engine issues experienced by some model years.   Fortunately some dealerships offer a lifetime powertrain warranty to cover this concern.    Also, the rear crash test rating is  POOR through MY 2025.  Yes, "POOR", as in "very bad"....  Not sure if that is fixed for MY2026, but something to consider/research if you frequently carry rear passengers.  

Final point, not sure why you guys are pushing the hybrids.  For most of these, you wont' make your hybrid upcharge in fuel savings until you reach 150k miles or more.   That does not even consider the interest you would have earned on the $5000 or so paid for a hybrid.   With modes investment success, you'd double your money every 10 years or so.   That means, you'd have to drive roughly 300,000 miles to get your money back.    Who drives 30,000 miles a year, anyway?.....  Rough math i know.... and some prefer to safe the evironment with batteries instead of coal, but from a financial point of view, hybrids makes little or no sense.

comment: Don't get the obsession by reviewers about the 'lack of buttons'.  After a few weeks or less, you get used to 'how to do things'. comment: Wow. You are 101 out of 103 reviews who complained about Kia's climate control screen. It is 2025, and I can't believe you still get it wrong. Let me explained it to you. For example, volume control you do that on the steering wheel. You want skip a song or go back to previous song, you do that on the steering wheel with your thumb without looking down. Everything else you do that on the main screen. Because Kia gives you access to two different functions in a screen, doesn't mean it is the main control point for both. I have 2024 EV6 with the same system and have not switched between screens. Mine stays as climate control 100% and I find it easy to use. And Kia's buttons , those you like, and toggle switches on the steering wheel are so good, why don't you like to use them? Especially these days all manufacturers put everything in one big screen. I really hope Kia keeps this separate screen for climate control.

video_title: We Tested Ten SUVs, Which One's the Best?
author: @richardausten5295
comment: Historically, Toyota and Honda have been the most reliable cars. But it depends on which models and times have changed. First-year models of a new generation score lower, and Toyota, in particular, have put out a slew of new cars. So their reliability dropped. Subaru ranked number one in December 2024 as the most reliable car brand overall - BMW was 2nd or 3rd, uncharacteristically for a German brand. But reliability is part of the equation - the dealer experience also matters. Reviewers at Savagegeese note the generally awful dealer experience with both Korean brands. You get a 10-year warranty that they won't honour - so what good is that? They have also had millions of 4-cylinder cars recalled for catching fire. Toyota has had all kinds of problems over the last couple of years. The Car Care Nut channel is terrific because he goes over all the cars with a fine-tooth comb, detailing all the problems from a mechanic's perspective, looking at all of the engine parts, the shocks, the transmission, and points out all the weak spots. He recently gave glowing takes on the Honda Passport and Hyundai Palisade. But he still points out their weak spots, like the VCM in the Passport and that they use a timing belt. He notes how difficult things will be to fix (which means more expensive) down the road. The dealer experience is critical - Kia Hynundai may be totally fine in your city and rubbish in another, ditto Honda or Toyota, etc. All cars eventually break down, so you want to be sure the dealer is going to do right by you.  Sometimes it may make more sense to choose the 3rd most reliable car if you know the dealer is rock solid over the 1st most reliable car when the dealership has a reputation of blaming you and not doing the repairs. While I have never owned Lexus - I generally hear the service is absolutely first rate.

video_title: Best Compact Car: 8-Car Mega Comparison
author: @jneedee
comment: Wow. As someone who is a DIYer and recently lost 10Gs on a bad Honda engine design, I'd like to expand a bit on these results... A car is much more than it's electronic gadgets, which in reality, creates really lazy and bad habits. Of ALL of the vehicles tested here, I find it misrepresentative of reality that the Nissan ends last in this test. It is the least gadgety and subjectively one of the top 2 best looking of the bunch. I recently test drove most of these vehicles and they all have jarring unexpected issues. Especially the lag on the VW and the crummy fabric inside the Honda. What's also surprising is that the Kia and the Hyundai finish so far apart given they practically the SAME vehicle at base. There is a lot of whine about how the Nissan falls behind on tech. Tech though, isn't trying to reconnect your phone multiple times or having so little adjustability in the driver assist controls. I think these are much more a nuisance and considerably more prone to issues than simply driving like a responsible citizen. Especially the cost when something goes wrong... And running costs is a HUGE consideration when you're rating on essentially what are "economy" minded vehicles. Any Turbo, no matter the recommendations, need to run on premium fuel in order to avoid issues - especially with the now common direct injection engines that build up carbon like nobody's business. And this adds a massive 35-50% to the cost of fuel alone, let alone the eventual Turbo rebuild. Essentially there are so many real world factors that go unconsidered in this comparison that it is unhelpful in any real way, and potentially misleading in others. I do however enjoy the in camera performance of the assessors. So thanks for that.

comment:
What a stupid comparison.  The civid hybrid is so much more expensive than most of the rest.  Compare a gas model Civic against the rest.  Another commenter was right, if you are adding the hybrid Civic to the comparison you need to add the si and GLI.

I've had 5 civics since 1995 up to 2018 and each time the quality dropped.  Bad quality brakes, engine problems, power steering rack failure and now an elevated price with no deals to be had.  Since then I had a 2019 GLI and the 2022 Jetta and now a 2026 Impreza RS.  I've had over 20 vehicles since 1995 so more than the average person.  Here are the highlights.

- 1995 Civic in manual lasted 180k km but did have engine gasket issues but that was at the end and I pushed that egine hard and never replaced the clutch.
- Used 2008 V6 Sport Rav4.  Had it for 5 years after I bought it used and put about 70k km.  No problems other than failing sunroof.  In the end the back seat was just too uncomfortable (seats too low) as the kids got bigger.
- 2007 Subaru Impreza: this was a tank in manual transmission.  Tried to get stuck in the snow but couldn't.   Not sure why I got rid of it to be honest.
- 2021 Tiguan - still have this and out of all the family size vehicles that I had (2001 Outback, 2007 Pilot, 2008 Odyssey, 2011 Forester, 2008 Rav4, 2017 Highlander, 2018 Santa Fe) the Tiguan is the Goldilocks of the group when considering space, power, handling, price, styling).  Luckily I had warranty for engine repair so we'll see how much lo ger I keep it considering powertrain warranty ends in August 2026.  This has been my favourit family hauler.
- 2019 GLI which I bought in 2021.   Felt fast when I first bought it and was fun to drive in manual.  Shifter was quite clunky until it warmed up in the winter and really poor traction even with winters.  Traded this in for a 2022 Jetta because the used market prices were crazy high and I got 8k more than I paid for my GLI one year later.   2022 Jetta had for 3 years and was on its 3rd set of rear brakes.  Sun glasses compartment failure (same as the tiguan) and steering  wheel had to be replace because of faulty sensors.  Really poor quality car and cheap radio and suspension. 
-2026 Subaru Impreza RS (Citron Yellow) - Traded in the leased 2002 Jetta and got $3300 in equit out of a car I put no money down on.  Early days but can without a doubt saythe best handling vehicle I have ever had.  The CVT surprising responsive  - doesntmake me miss my GLI.  Paddle shifters actually do something and "shifting" down actually slows down the vehicle similar to a manual where you often dont need to brake - unlike other brands that have 'manual mode' that just make the engine louder - talking about you Hyundai.

In the end,  Civics are not as good as they used to be and Honda is relying on past reputation.  They aren't bad cars but they don't justify their crazy prices nor fiance rates.  There are better cars out there with better deals to be had.  

I'm paying $380 taxes in on a Impreza RS lease.  Tell me where you can find a car of this quality for that price today  - CDN dollars.

author: @blueBruSea
comment:
I had a 22 Mazda3 sedan in the premium plus turbo trim and there were a lot of things I loved about it. What made me trade it in for my 25 Civic Hybrid ST was the fuel efficiency, ride quality, and interior/cargo space. 

The Mazda felt luxurious on the inside, until you hit even slightly rough roads. I can still feel the shakes on the highway that night. What drove me up the wall was it's less than reported MPG. With that turbo, I was happy to see 24mpg combined, but most of the time I got 21. Combine that with a small tank meant regular fuel ups every 1 to 1.5 weeks. 

The Civic, especially in the hatchback option, checked all the boxes I needed. Spacious, fun to drive, speedy, and fuel efficient. What do I miss on the Mazda? The 360 camera, lumbar support, and honestly, the infotainment. I love that dial. But it wasn't worth the rough ride and constant fuel ups on what is supposed to be a commuter compact, not a sports car.

I found the Honda the easiest to deal with as far as enough technology, comfort, looks, roominess and look. I also disagree about the Honda’s info system. comment:
All of these are good cars.  Really today there are no bad ones just some better than others but more I believe that one car that one person likes and rates number 1 another person may not like and rate last.  Everyone has their own like and dislikes on audio screens, interior layouts, styling, engine and transmission type and power and driving dynamics.  

For example my order would be totally different than this.  My pick would be a Nissan Sentra SR in Atlantic Gray with the Black Roof and the 2 tone alloys that the SR comes standard with.  Why?  I like the styling of it inside and out its more old school.  I hate panoramic roofs and like the standard sunroof on the Sentra and my one must have features are a 360 camera and heated steering wheel and it has both.  I may be partial to Nissan as I own a 2023 Nissan Kicks SR with Premium Package that I purchased new in October 2023 and it was by far the best equipped CUV I could find for $26,000.00 and is fully loaded.  Many cars and CUVs over $30,000.00 did not have the safety and convenience features it came with.  I also prefer a naturally aspirated engine for simplicity and reliability.  

I was not interested in waiting on the upcoming new generation 2025 Nissan Kicks as first year models always have issues for the first year or two until they work out any bugs.  Just like 2024 Chevy Trax having electrical issues, engine failures, power window failures, screen glitches and more but for 2025 there were less issues with the Trax and for 2026 most should be worked out of the Trax.  I was an avid Mitsubishi fan and owned 6 Mitsubishis all in top trim fully equipped (3 Mirages, 1 Outlander Sport and 2 Eclipse Crosses) and never had a single issue with any.  Our 2019 Mitsubishi Eclipse Cross SEL Touring will be 6 years old this October and have not had 1 issue and it also has the Jatco CVT (Nissan and Mitsubishi use Jatco) and has been trouble free like all of our others.  Do the maintenance and the car will last.  Yes older generation Jatco CVTs had many issues but they have all been resolved in the current Nissan and Mitsubishis.  

But my top 3 picks and trims for each model would be…

1. Nissan Sentra SR with Premium Package

2. Toyota Corolla XSE Hybrid AWD

3. Kia K4 GT-Line (non turbo)

One of my Favorite interiors and interior colors in this video is the Elantra but I don’t like the exterior design or that it has a dual clutch transmission.  

My least favorite would probably be the Mazda 3 mainly due to its far away audio screen and that during driving you mostly have to use the dial and buttons to control the audio.  I think its sharp looking inside out just don’t like the audio design.

comment:
This is a great video with wonderful information, but the AI "narrator" is off on some things (IN-teh-gra - nope In-TEH-gra). I also wouldn't call an I-4 engine in such surplatives, unless the car really deserves it (e.g., close to 400hp, 350 lb/ft). the turbocharged inline 4 is in most small cars - and, sadly more in mid-sized cars.

The Audi RS series is interesting: regardless of the model (RS3, RS4, RS5, RS7...) they all have comparable numbers. 0-60? Around 3.5 seconds (thanks to amazing engines mostly shipped from the Porsche factory in Stuttgart and the rally-tried Quattro AWD). Top Speed? About 175mph. But, hands down, they have been the most exciting cars that I can afford to drive (and service). To note: the RS5 has the same 2.9l V6 that's in the Porsche Cayenne S and Panamera S, but Audi tuned it up, raising the 375hp to 444hp for the RS5.

And I don't think the Mercedes C63 is powered by a 4-cylinder. I think it has the hand-built biturbo V8 that is standard in all AMG 63 series. The price tag helps explain the difference between the C53 and the C63 (or C63S).

author: @michaeldeloach838
comment: I'm one of those that believe a muscle car is basically an American car that has a high horsepower high torque V8 under the hood. Originally there was a difference between a true muscle car and a pony car, mainly the engine size and HP output. Also the size of the car. Muscle cars were bigger and had bigger engines and more HP. That changed in the latter part of the 60s and very early 70s when they started putting big blocks in pony cars which made them also muscle cars. Even the corvette sports car got big block power making it also a muscle car. The lines got blurred. Pony cars and even a sports car became muscle cars while also still being pony cars and a sports car. Today the lines are still blurred. Even though today's pony cars have mostly all small block motors they're putting out insane amounts of power with superchargers, turbos, nitrous, etc. Lots of V8 horsepower and torque is what makes any American car a muscle car in my book. Not everyone agrees and that's OK. But today's American performance cars have multiple labels. Pony cars, muscle cars, sports cars, sport sedans, and the new Corvette C8 and Ford GT are arguably super cars. Call it what you want, just drive it like you stole it

author: @WTRGK
comment:
Okay okay okay, I don't think many people will agree with me, but hear me out here.

I own a final model ford falcon, XR6, it's a sport ute with a stick shift. Fun as, not particularly fast though. No turbo, but may boost her in the future.

I consider it to be a pony car since other falcons (XR8, GT-F, Pursuit ute, so on) have big Barra and Boss V8 motors under the hood, and my ute is like the baby brother of those bigger muscle cars.

As I said, mine is not by any means a beast. It pumps out about 195kw (261hp) and 391nm of torque from a 4.0L straight six. Rear drive too, baby.

Turbo ones were available from factory, however I am a new-ish driver on my second year of a probationary licence, and am not yet legally allowed to own a car that puts out (I believe) 300+ hp. So no turbo for me yet.

I bought it at a fairly chunky sum for someone my age, but being a ute, I have access to the HUGE back tray and it's still sporty enough to rip around twisties when I want to. If you're so inclined, yes, you can easily kick the back end out. The low end torque is very good with this motor.

I will probably move on to a more powerful vehicle after paying this one off, sure, but for the time being, I see it as a pony (or sports) car, and a nod of respect to its turbo six and V8 variants.

I get a bit of crap for what bought it for, being a naturally aspirated six, but I wish that weren't the case. I'm as much of a driver and an enthusiast as the next person. I love the falcon platform.

In my eyes, my ute is a little slice of the bigger musclebois and thus, a pony car.

author: @GTX1123
comment: In 1977 you would be LAUGHED at if you referred to anything with a small block as a muscle car. Mustangs, Camaros, Corvettes, late 60's Barracudas, Plymouth Dusters, Dodge Demons, Dodge Swingers were by and large the pony cars of the day. The REAL muscle cars had big blocks and were as follows ; Mopar - 383 Magnum, 426 Hemi, 440 sixpack (Cuda, Challenger, Charger, GTX, Roadrunner, Satellite) Ford - 390, 460, 429 Cobra Jet (Torino, Galaxy, Shelby) Chevy - 396, 427, 454 (Chevelle, Impala, Nova). Olds, Buick, Pontiac and of course Cadillac also had options for big blocks as well (389, 455 and a 500 CI for Cadillac). There were also options with the Corvette for the 427 Rat motor and limited big block editions of the Mustang (429) Dodge Swinger (440) etc.

author: @TitaniumCountess
comment: I would apply the "muscle car" term pretty liberally. I even consider my own ride to be a "muscle car". The "pony car" term - I'd apply that to the Mustang 4-cylinder, the V6 Camaro, and possibly the Subaru BRZ - rear drive 'sporty' car aimed at the youth population. "Muscle Car" is much more encompassing - rear drive, big horsepower. Some Mustangs clearly fall into the Muscle Car category, the Challenger of course, the V8 Camaros - and also things like some of the Mercedes AMGs fall into the Muscle Car category - the V8 powered E55/E63, C63, etc - those are clearly modern day interpretations of "muscle cars". I wouldn't include the BMW M cars in the "muscle" category as they have a completely different character, making horsepower at high RPMs... they are full fledged "sports cars", which is a third category. Pony Cars have mostly died out, replaced by Sports Cars and Muscle Cars.

author: @Flakey86
comment:
Here is my take on the mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive list of sporty CAR types: 

-Hypercar: the top echelon of sports cars produced in modern eras, must use exotic materials, processes, technology. Sole focus is performance, which surpasses most race cars of the time. 

-Supercar: Sports cars with increased focus on acceleration and top speed. Typically use exotic materials, processes and technology. Typically beyond financial reach of middle class households.

-Sportscar: A car whose primary focus is on handling, braking and enjoyable driving dynamics. Typcially affordable by of-age middle class households. Almost exclusively limited to two useful seats. Offers straight line performance above most cars in lower tiers but there are edge cases where this is not the case. EG: Corvette, 911, Jag F type, 370Z 

-GT Car: A sporty car with significant luggage capacity. Focus is less on outright dynamics, prioritizing enough comfort to make long drives pleasant. Often trades cornering/braking performance for highway-usable power. More expensive than muscle and pony cars which have similar characteristics. EG: //M cars, AMG cars, Aston Martins

-Sports luxury: Lower-priced GT cars which attempt to mimic the luxurious and sporting attributes of GT cars while typically offering less outright power. EG: Inifiniti G37, Lexus RC350, 228I Msport, Audi S3

-Muscle Car: The inverse of a sports car, prioritizing straight-line speed over cornering ability. Typically coupes built on full-size frames with four usable seats. Considerably more affordable than GT cars, but generally worse handling characteristics and quality. US/AUS manufacturers. Almost exclusively V8 powered. EG: Challenger, Charger, Chevy SS, Holden Monaro.

-Pony Car: Compact affordable coupes patterned after the ford mustang model, targeted to young adults. Prioritizes fun over other attributes. Typcically fall on the spectrum between Sports, GT and Muscle cars. EG: Ford Mustang, Chevy Camaro, Genesis Coupe

-Rally-like cars: Compact four wheel drive performance cars which specialize in all weather and road condition performance. Patterned after the Subaru WRX and Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution. Typically powered by turbocharged four cylinder engines. EG: WRX, EVO 

-Roadster: Sporty two-seater convertibles prioritizing driving fun and light weight over all other factors. Patterned after British compact sporty convertibles. EG: Mazda MX5

-Hot Hatch: Compact and highly affordable performance cars. Typically front wheel drive with four cylinder powerplants which may be turbocharged. 3 or 5 doors.

comment: These days, terms like "muscle car" and "pony car" seem more like advertising speak - similar to "retro" styling - that harks back to that era so many people think of as the Golden Age of cars.  Performance cars of today are much more sophisticated than in the past...the emphasis may be on straight line speed in some cases, but they can actually turn a corner occasionally.  Considering cost (pony cars were originally aimed at a young market - who usually don't have all that much money)...I would say that the equivalent of a pony car these days would be the Subaru BRZ (or the Toyota GT86/Scion FRS branded version), or maybe the Miata MX-5as they are sporty by today's standards, not exactly slow - but lacking the brute horsepower of larger performance vehicles, handle better than most large cars, have a relatively low cost...and still RWD.  Today's equivalent to a muscle car...would be any large, car with an option from the factory to get a huge engine jammed under the hood - with virtually no improvements to the suspension or brakes (a bit of a rarity these days, what with people taking more interest in safety than in previous decades.)  But that's just what I think...anyone else see it differently?  :-)

To be fair, buying a new car and selling it two years later, is never a good deal. I generally keep my cars four year and sell them on for about half the MSRP. That works for me, because I get to enjoy the car for a good while and have adventures with it.

But if you can find what you are looking for on the used car market, with about 4-6 years under their belt and in good nick, you will be much better off in terms of depreciation.

I bought a used 2017 Jaguar F-Type V6 a couple of years ago and sold a Porsche Cayman S from the 987 generation for it. Both are great cars to drive. The Cayman S is the more communicative experience for skilled drivers. The F-Type is the more refined experience and is better judged for daily driving without it urging you on all the time. I respect the Cayman, but I love the F-Type.

comment:
I have instructed for the past 10yrs and been in all of these cars except the Bite My Weiner...thankfully.  The only TRUE Sports car with a genuine Carbon Fiber tub is the 4C. Everything else weighs at least 1000lbs more guys.  The 21st century is giving us nothing but obese muscle cars....VERY SAD.  Elise and 4c are probably the last of their breed.  It is DROP DEAD Gorgeous from any angle.  No sound proofing, raw, manual steering.  You couldn't shift from 1st to 2nd fast enough if you tried so the DCT is 100% fitting.

It needed AWD because it was so diabolical with RWD only.  My 2012 XK was far prettier btw, but was a lousy highway car with its overly stiff, jittery rear suspension. Ian Callum nailed that design.  My Maserati GTS blew the F Type away .......and handled shockingly well on track even in a pro driver's hands that got out and looked at me saying "I had no idea it was this good".

Corvette is the closest thing to a true sports car America makes.  C7 was its best effort but the weight gain from the c6Z06 was unacceptable...and they still sucked in the rain....hallmark of a great handling car.

Mustang GT350 was an extraordinary motor on a bloated body.  Can't believe new M2's are just as obese as a Mustang.  My worst day teaching last year was in a 2022 M4Comp.  Fat, lethargic, crazy power but very unrewarding to teach someone in.  Nuff said here.  Take 500+lbs and a foot off the Mustang and that could be my top choice.

We are NOT living in a great era for the sports car.  Even the german recipe is modeling the Americans now with when in doubt add more HP to counter the weight gain.  Most new cars are LOUSY to teach in sadly.  Long live the REAL sports cars like Miata, GR86, BRZ, Elise and the only one with a SUPERCAR CARBON FIBER chassis.....yup the Alfa 4C!!!! LUltra low mileage final editions with red CF tubs are selliing deep into the 150K +++ zone already.  That should tell you something.  None of the those other cars carries that upside.

If I want the look at me old man's relatively sedate car in the group, the Jag would get the nod...but I have an Alfa Romeo Stelvio Quad that will eat it for lunch and only weights 200-lbs more!....with 580HP hehe. so it can haul a$$ and the bacon too.

Finally, I drove my 4C Spider 2910 miles cross country with a track day stop at Pitt International Raceway with my wife.......no Nacy boy need cushy for me...remember its a REAL sports car

comment:
I think the i8 looks great, aside from it looking like it is birthing a 911 out the back end. (No, really, look!) For daily driving, in CA, with high gas prices, the i8 gives you exotic looks, great mpg, scissor doors, and half the people won’t even know what it is.  The biggest drawback of owning one would be I have no idea what the maintenance/repairs would be like. It’s a low production exotic hybrid. I could see going to start it one day, and a light comes on the dash, and it’s a 5 figure repair job!  

So, out of those 5 choices, the one I would choose would be the GT350.  Just drive it with a big smile on your face all the time.  Love it. (I have an S197 Roush…) Planned to get one “once prices came down” on used ones, but those prices haven’t come down.  I should rent one sometime and just hit the canyons with it for a day - but then I’ll just want to buy one even more!  And my Roush is fun! But that GT350… chef’s kiss.  

Oh, and fwiw, the C5 felt like a 90’s car. An evolution over the C4, but the C6 definitely was a revolution. Very 2000’s feeling - which now is 20 years ago, so NOT modern, but definitely not 90’s. Have owned plenty of 90’s cars, and driven the C5 and C6.  The C6 was such an improvement, and honestly, at current prices, no excuse not to own one if you want to feel what a V8 American sports car is like. Buy it for the driving enjoyment, not for anything else. It’s like a big Miata, and I don’t mean like an NC. 😅

author: @nigel.w
comment:
In Canada, I'd buy either of the two Americans if available for 50k Canadian dollars. But I live in the UK, and for that money it would be a choice between a regular Mustang GT, F-Type V6 S, base 981 Cayman, and a 997.1 911. For me, it would be between the F-Type and the 911. If I wanted an auto it would be the F-Type -- although you can get a manual F-Type for the money -- and if I wanted a manual it would be the 911.

Neither of the two Americans is available in right-hand drive, so would rule them out for most people in the UK, including myself. And neither can be had for anywhere near CAD50k. You also couldn't get a 4C or an i8 for that money in the UK. And you'd also be 'lucky' to get a high mileage V8 F-Type for the money.

The F-Type is good value to buy but they have proven quite needy and aren't in any way cheap to own or maintain. Most petrolheads in the UK would opt for a base 981 Cayman.

IMO, the main downside of the F-Type is what most people think is one of its most compelling features, ie, the engines. For me, the artificially engineered pops and bangs are annoying to live with, and the engines are all poorly designed, which isn't what you want in the longer term. 

I suspect the C7 Corvette will always be desirable, not least for its relative simplicity, and the GT350 will always be desirable simply because of its special engine. Both a good-looking cars, too.

The i8's drivetrain is also something you're not going to want in the longer term. And the 4C, at least here in the UK where the roads are terrible, is far too punishing to live with unless it's just for a Sunday morning blast, and as acknowledged we have the Alpine A110, which would be most people's choice as an alternative to a Cayman or an F-Type in the UK.

comment:
I’ve owned both the i8 and the 4C, so I can speak from experience. The i8 definitely turns heads and is a lot of fun in a straight line. However, it didn’t feel that exciting in the corners. Before tuning, it felt a bit too predictable—like an electric car, it responded the same way every time you hit the throttle. After getting it tuned and adding a custom turbo-back exhaust, the car really came alive, and I started enjoying it much more.

But the car I loved the most is the 4C. It was raw, loud, and razor-sharp in its handling. People even mistook it for a Ferrari at times. Out of everything I’ve owned, the 4C is still my favorite. I can’t wait to get another one. It was so responsive and always put a huge smile on my face. It just felt truly special—unlike anything else on the road.

author: @AlexRMcColl
comment: "when it's really loaded in a corner, it's great." 13:07. 4C owner living in Calgary here, this is a Toronto problem, not a 4C problem. On a mountain road outside of Calgary, I love my 4C. Corner after grin inducing corner. All the other issues are fair, but can be mitigated significantly with a good alignment, proper tire pressures, and upgrading to Cup 2 tires. The difference is surprising. A 4C with a poor alignment and slightly underinflated tires will tram a lot more than one with a good alignment and good pressure (the dash will still say "OK" because the pressure is safe to drive, but the tramlining will be worse). Yes, the radio is terrible, but one of the benefits of it being a cheap drop in is that you can buy a cheap replacement. I replaced mine with a small car-play supporting touch screen from Joying that even made the speakers sound better. All that being said, back when I lived in Toronto I was thinking F-Type and I would sell the 4C and buy an F-Type if I moved away from the mountains. Best of luck with the Grand Tour.

video_title: $50,000 Used Question // GT350 vs Alfa 4C vs BMW i8 vs F Type R vs Corvette Z51
author: @Biltware
comment:
Two and a half years ago, I was literally the target audience for this video. I was looking for a 2-door sports car and had a budget of $50-60k. I literally had on my short list three of the five cars you guys tested: the C7 Vette, the F-Type R, and the GT350. Here's why I passed on each one of them.

1) The C7 was just "too sporty" for me. It was too low to the ground, had too tight of a cockpit, and didn't have a dedicated trunk. I wanted more of a "grand touring" car, and less of a true "sports" car.
2) The F-Type R wasn't available with a manual transmission. That was a huge buzzkill. A manual was Priority 1 while shopping for my next car. Otherwise, it looked amazing, sounded amazing, and had a very comfortable cockpit. No separate trunk, but I was so smitten with its looks that I didn't care. Jaguar long-term reliability was also a concern however.
3) I was REALLY close to getting a GT350. Having owned a 2015 GT in the past, I was partial to the Mustang. However,  I would only have bought a 2019 or 2020 model due to the changes Ford made to the Voodoo engine and oil system after 2018. Unfortunately, every GT350 from those two model years I found within a few hundred miles of me with less than 10k miles also had an asking price north of $65k and even $70k. I could have easily bought a 2016 or 2017, but worried so much about the engine issues that I couldn't pull the trigger.

So after all that, I eventually ended up buying a 2022 Mustang Mach 1. It had just 700 miles on it during my test drive, so I saved a bundle over buying new. It had the reliability and sound of the Coyote V8, and the buttery-smooth Tremec transmission from the Shelby. Add in the digital gauge cluster, rev-matching, and all the parts from the GT350 and GT500, and it was the perfect car for me in the end. I paid $57k for it (MSRP was $63k), and after two years and 15,000 miles later, I could still sell it for around $50k today no problem. Sure, the GT350 has the Voodoo engine and you get to be part of the "Shelby club" and all that, but I love every minute I spend behind the wheel of the Mach 1. No regrets whatsoever.

comment: I personally owned a 4C for about a year & a half! fun car to drive but boy is it absolutely annoying once you nitpick it! Has one vent only on the driver side, Drain plug is permanently mated to the oil pan so it only unscrews & comes out far enough to drain that is AFTER you remove the annoying belly pan! All manual input steering(no power steering), washer fluid reservoir fill tube is located under the driver wiper blade & requires some funky work to access! The automatic is NOT an automatic it's a duel clutch manual transmission that will fight you in stop & go traffic & can easily burn them up if you constantly creep forwards in traffic at stops! I've learned to just stop & stay stopped. U turns are impossible at slow speeds because it has no power steering. All in all yes it's pretty cheap here in the states vs a fully kitted Tahoe or whatever but maintaining such a vehicle is not worth it! For me it’s very simple. I don’t want to own a decade old Jaguar F-Type R or BMW i8 out of warranty. Expensive out of warranty used Jaguars or BMW’s are a financial suicide unless you know how to fix your own cars and then even it’s iffy. 
Based on that I have not heard great things about reliability of GT350 gen 1 versions either. I like that car a lot, but another reliability nightmare hassle I don’t care to worry about. Same thing for Alfa Romeo…Alfa’s reliability is usually its Achilles heel. 

By default that makes C7 Z51 the right choice. It’s not necessarily a reliability nightmare to own. 

But honestly at this point I think you are better off spending $5-10k more and get yourself a low mileage M2 or Supra or Nissan Z or even a decent C8 that is still under factory warranty.

video_title: $50,000 Used Question // GT350 vs Alfa 4C vs BMW i8 vs F Type R vs Corvette Z51
author: @arnoldmiga5689
comment: One thing is how they drive and another thing is the ownership experience including depreciation and ease of repairs. After owning a few fun cars to date, I concluded that as these cars get older, the simpler they are the better. Forget about that i8, it will make you reconsider your life choices. Before buying, check prices of parts, they can be eye watering...if the parts are available at all. For that reason, based on personal experience, to keep ownership cost low at higher mileages and due to the age of the components and to keep cost of repairs low, I concluded to never own anymore anything exotic (e.g. older maserati), anything with mid-engine, 4WD, transaxle, automatic, adjustable shocks, direct injection (i.e. one injector for N54 BMW engine is $500, you'll need 6 and they don't last). Ideally a car from pre-electronically controlled thermostats and pre-electric water pumps as well (one failed on me 1000 km from home on a winter night). Best if with timing belt (far easier to replace the belt than timing chains with their brittle plastic tensioners). Believe me, peeling layers of parts from the engine bay of my BMW e89 to replace a $5 gasket gets old very quickly and it's no fun at all. Oh and never again a car without a spare wheel, guess how I learned this one.

author: @CentaXBerlin2
comment:
Wow! I really appreciate your reviews and your views on cars. This one hits so close to home, because a few months ago I bought a 2013 F-Type V8 S convertible in Salsa Red for kind of the same reasons. I wanted the most hardcore RWD version; the V8 R convertible is incredible rare, which was too much of a premium (and actually hard to find) on the used market. Why a convertible? Because you get 200% more sound and involvement. The F-Type was a classical "Hero Car". When Tata bought JLR, they needed to make a statement. So they finally build a proper sports car and dared to name it the E-Type successor. The F-Types objective was not to boost revenue, but to build the company image. No expenses spared, probably. 

I wanted a V8 for many years. Looked at W213 C63s first, they sell for around ~40k€. Insurance kills you however, and they will continue to depreciate as there are a lot. One day it clicked; I don't need practicality now, I can trade the practicability for something way more unique. 

I don't think the F-Type will continue to depreciate. I rather think the contrary. The exhaust is crazy; mine never had a software update, tuning down the pops and bangs. It is registered to 112dB noise level, stock. There is hardly anything louder, as during this time, there was a loophole using valved exhaust systems. The RWD is quite rare. There is no need for more power, it can hardly lay it down in 2nd gear, full traction is only in 3rd - but if it's just slightly wet or slippery, sometimes the rear will slightly slide at 120+km/h. It's something so extreme, which makes it so entertaining and challenging also in the long-term. Sure the AWD is faster, but powersliding every corner and the ability to rebalance in each corner with the instantaneous throttle response is just incredible fun. I can't stay composed in this car, I still laugh manic exactly like you every time I drive it.

But all of that is only when you push it. You can deflate the seats side cushions, put it in D, disengage Dynamic Mode - and it has a fully switched personality. It's relaxing and comfortable, a cruiser that you could daily drive. With retrofitted Android Auto I miss nothing in it.

The cars it was compared against back in the day are for sure better sports cars or better cars overall, but depreciation is your friend. I would not prefer the Vantage V8 to the F-Type; the old Vantage actually has a Jaguar AJ37 non-supercharged V8 and many interior parts from my prior 2006 Volvo C30. Sure it's a nice car that will age well and looks great, but I think the Jaguar gives the better package with the worse badge. I don't care, there is not a single car I would trade my F-Type for.

Owning the F-Type, this car is soo much more than I hoped for. Not just the engine, response, sounds, but also the luxury, refinement, handling, looks. I actually think the V6S is even more bang-for-your-buck, you can get one starting at ~33k€ in germany; you still get thrilling sound, it's just not quite as mental as the V8.

I disagree wholeheartedly on the Jag F type.  I don't think it has aged well.  It looks very "early 2000's" to me.  Also, the sound is loud and burbly, but it also sounds unrefined and artificial. The Alfa Romeo feels like "This guy spent way too much money on an inferior 4 cylinder just because he has some eurofantasy about italian cars".  Yes, a lot of old guys drive Corvettes, and a lot of teen boys drive Mustangs, but those two cars sound CLEARLY better than the rest and they both offer way more performance (and reliability) dollar for dollar.  They are the smart purchase.

I used to own a 2014 c7 z51 and I loved every bit of it.. except the automatic transmission. One day I'll get another one.

comment: All interesting and cool cars and a really interesting video. For the ones intersted: The way to make an i8 drive better is by radically changing the wheels. Either you buy it for the look and how it makes you feel or just go for a different car. There is no objectively good reason for the i8 and any single one category. It's not crazy fast, not crazy good at handling, not a crazy good hybrid and so on. But it's special and a absolute head turner. For the presented i8 here: Not a fan of the added body parts (the little  carbon fiber winglets on the front skirt for example) - ruins the look a little bit in my opinion. author: @pulixpulix2420
comment:
My order is: 

No #4 Lexus
No #3 Audi
No #2 & No #1 Mercedes and BMW <-- a tie

No #4 Lexus --> Because it has the least amount of technology in it. Mainly in the infotainment system and also engine. Low resolution, small screen, low CPU, lower quality materials (plastic & leather), worse gearbox and the MOST EXPENSIVE of the 4. That is a big show stopper because if it's 5.000 pounds more expensive. It should deliver. It doesn't. I won't pay 5000 extra just to be unique and not go for 'german', right? 

No #3 Audi --> Very well build, I would say that there is almost no difference between the 3 (Audi, Merc & BMW) in the build quality of the materials (leather and plastics). Audi has that DSG which sometimes has lag and also that weight distribution problem being so damn heavy in the front. The Google contract saved them because the Audi infotainment system sucked BIG TIME before. Now, with Google on your map and on your gauges it's a big step forward. Still a very good car but I have to agree with Mat on the design. From my point of view it looks like a Ford Mondeo in the front. 

No#2 & No#1 A tie --> from the technological point of view it's a tie, although I love the BMW's gearbox and also the iDrive is above the Merc's. But, I agree with the looks of the Mercedes (exterior and interior) are much nicer than the BMW's. Both cars have an exceptional driving dynamics at high speeds and also in corners. I would choose the BMW but it's just a matter of taste. And forget about the all wheel drive at all of these cars. They are meant to be driven raw, without the 'handicap' of 4x4. comment: I'm 21 and picked up my C Class Coupe 4 months ago, my first Mercedes, so hopefully I can offer a bit of owner experience! First of all, opinions on the looks are just that........opinions. Some people like the Coupe, some don't, you'll get that with any car! I agree, I prefer to look at the car from the front because the diamond grille and chrome splitter really sets it off, but then I like the back because it's clearly been based off the S Class, a car waaaay out of my price range and a lot of others too. Then there's the interior, the best part of the car for me. Mine is the obsidian black metallic exterior, with the beige/cream artico leather interior, complete with the same black ash wood console in the video which, in my opinion (again, entirely subjective), is the best interior in its class at the moment. Its hard to believe that such an interior is available in a car in this price range, of which mine was just above £42000 as has a multitude of options. It's the C250d with the 2.1 diesel and 9 speed auto (of which is a fantastic gearbox), I'm returning on average 55mpg at the moment after 2500 miles. My one hate about the car though? How unrefined the diesel engine sounds. Going along its absolutely fine and you can't tell you sound like you're driving a tractor haha! It's when you are at idle or come to a stop that it's bad. But then the cabin is so quiet that you do well to hear anything outside of it! Acceleration? It isn't slow by any means, a multitude of torque helps with that and in the real world you'd do well to tell the difference between any of the cars tested. Honestly, I was surprised at how well it handles corners, especially in Sport but push a bit more and you start to understeer a bit; characteristics of a heavy Mercedes I would have thought!
